game.name: Chess
game.description: Chess is a game for two players on a board of sixty-four squares. Each player starts with sixteen pieces and tries to checkmate the enemy king.

vocabulary.means: It names one of the sixteen men a player controls. A pawn is a piece too, unless a sentence sets pawns apart from the other pieces on purpose.
It names one of the sixty-four places on the board.
It names one player's single act of taking a piece from one square to another.
It names the removal of an enemy piece by a piece that lands on its square.
It names a game that ends with no winner. Stalemate is one kind of draw, and not a word for every draw.
It names the player who controls the light pieces and moves first.

textFields.describes: how the piece moves and captures
the rules that apply only to this piece, such as castling or promotion

tokens.syntax: A piece letter in brackets, such as [K], or a square and a move written in plain algebraic notation, such as e4 and Nf3

answer: Rule text and rule numbers from the Laws of Chess.
Defined terms, such as castling, en passant, stalemate, and zugzwang.
Whether a stated move is legal, and why the rules allow it or refuse it.
How a game ends: checkmate, resignation, time, and every kind of draw.
How to write a move and how to keep a scoresheet.
Rule structure: parent rules, sub-rules, related rules, and the sections of the book.
Clock rules, time controls, touch-move, and the role of the arbiter.
refuse: Opening theory, engine evaluation, and advice on which move is stronger.
Ratings, titles, tournament results, and the history of matches between real players.
The rules of chess variants, such as three-check or Chess960, which this book does not cover.

extraGuidance: This corpus holds no cards. Chess has pieces, and a piece has no printed text. Do not offer a card lookup and do not describe a piece as a card.
Rule numbers run from 100 to 800 in one book. A number that ends in a bare hundred, such as 100 or 500, is a section heading with no text of its own; quote the numbered rule under it instead.
Name the exact rule number for every claim about legality. A reader who asks whether a move is legal needs the rule, not only the verdict.
Keep stalemate and checkmate apart in every answer. Both need a player with no legal move; only checkmate needs the king to be under attack.
A draw by repetition and a draw by the fifty-move count need a claim from a player. The fivefold and seventy-five-move forms need no claim. State which form applies.
